newsitem.title: CHINA: Friction seen between China military, party chief.
newsitem.headline: Friction seen between China military, party chief.

text.p: Strains are emerging between China's top military brass and Communist Party leaders as the ruling elite jostle for power and position in the run-up to a key party congress this year, Chinese sources said on Tuesday.

The cracks between veteran top officers of the People's Liberation Army loyal to late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, and Deng's successor, President Jiang Zemin, have been created by disputes over both policy and personnel, said sources close to the military, who declined to be identified.

Jiang's decision to sign a strategic partnership with Russia was the most recent source of friction with powerful military veteran General Liu Huaqing, senior vice chairman of the party's Central Military Commission, a member of the seven-member Politburo Standing Committee and close ally of Deng, the sources said.
The signing of the partnership by Jiang and his Russian counterpart Boris Yeltsin was the highlight of Jiang's visit to Moscow last month.
"The People's Liberation Army feels that whether China signed or didn't sign was all the same," said one source with close links to the military.

"China will not be a threat to the rest of the world in the next 10 to 20 years so it really didn't matter if we signed such an alliance with Yeltsin," the source said. "So what was the need to sign?"

China's top military brass regarded the partnership as bringing advantages to Russia in its tussle over expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), but serving little use to Beijing's interests, the sources said.

The view differs widely from that of Jiang, who is also head of the Communist Party and chairman of the Central Military Commission, and is eager to boost both his own personal standing and that of Beijing on the international stage, diplomats say.
"This means China has again become a card in the game," one source said, referring to the partnership.

After Beijing's socialist alliance with the Soviet Union broke up in the early 1960s amid rivalry for leadership of the communist world and territorial disputes, China has been careful to pursue an independent foreign policy.
Foreign policy differences were not the only divisive factor between the top military and the party chief, sources said.

Liu Huaqing, 81, and the sole representative of the three-million-strong People's Liberation Army in the Politburo or its standing committee, is expected to step down at the 15th Party Congress -- scheduled for October or November -- but is reluctant to go, the sources said.

Liu and Zhang Zhen, 83, second vice-chairman of the military commission and also expected to retire, have launched a stream of personnel appointments in the military to ensure a network of influence through their proteges even after they step down, said another military source.

On personnel, Jiang and Liu have already locked horns over whether the two elderly military generals should step down from the military commission -- and whether they should be replaced if they do retire, the source said.

Jiang is keen for Liu to step down, but Liu is reluctant to give the go-ahead to promotion of two more military commission vice-chairmen after the infighting that dogged the appointment of the two other current vice chairmen -- Jiang's protege General Chi Haotian and Liu's favoured Zhang Wannian.
In a compromise reached in a previous round, Chi Haotian, 68, was appointed vice-chairman -- but only in fourth position after Zhang Wannian, 69, whom he outranks in military seniority.

China's military, eased out of politics in the 1970s and 1980s, has commanded seats in the party's Politburo since it helped the government by crushing student-led pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June 1989.
